extracted.intended_audience: graduate and advanced-undergraduate students in algebraic geometry / category theory; readers of the textbook 'The Rising Sea'
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter giving foundational definitions, universal-property characterizations, important examples, and exercises in category theory relevant to algebraic geometry (products, pullbacks, localizations, tensor products, limits/colimits, adjoints, Yoneda).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A covariant functor F : A -> B is an equivalence of categories if it is fully faithful and every object of B is isomorphic to an object of the form F(A) for some A (F is essentially surjective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a functor has a quasiinverse G : B -> A (unique up to unique isomorphism) with G∘F ≅ id_A and F∘G ≅ id_B. Conversely any functor with a quasiinverse is an equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal properties determine objects up to unique isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: If an object is defined by a universal property, then (if it exists) it is essentially unique, i.e., unique up to unique isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: first show uniqueness up to unique iso, then construct an example to prove existence. Convention: we often say 'the' rather than 'a' for such objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product (universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Products are defined by a universal property in any category; products, if they exist, are unique up to unique isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to §1.1 discussion. Exercise: verify the product notion in any category and uniqueness up to unique isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial, final, and zero objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial object: an object with precisely one map to every object. Final object: an object with precisely one map from every object. Zero object: both initial and final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises show any two initial (resp. final) objects are uniquely isomorphic; motivates using 'the initial object'. Examples requested for Sets, Rings, Top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization of rings (universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a multiplicative subset S of a ring A, S^{-1}A with the canonical map A -> S^{-1}A is initial among A-algebras B in which every element of S maps to an invertible element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive description: elements a/s with fraction relations; important flavors Af (S={1,f,f^2,...}) and A_p (S=A\p). Exercise: A->S^{-1}A injective iff S contains no zerodivisors. Use the universal property to prove properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization of modules (universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an A-module M and multiplicative S, the map φ: M -> S^{-1}M is initial among A-module maps M -> N for which s: N -> N is an isomorphism for all s in S (i.e., elements of S act invertibly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: elements m/s with relations s(s2 m1 - s1 m2) = 0; S^{-1}M inherits S^{-1}A-module structure. Exercises to construct and verify universal property and map uniqueness up to iso.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product (universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A-modules M and N, M ⊗_A N is an A-module together with an A-bilinear map t: M × N → M ⊗_A N such that any A-bilinear map M × N → T factors uniquely through a unique A-linear map M ⊗_A N → T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructively: quotient of free module on M × N by bilinearity relations. Exercises: check universal property, uniqueness up to unique isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right-exactness of tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: The functor (–) ⊗_A N : Mod_A -> Mod_A is right-exact: it preserves surjections and the tail of exact sequences (i.e., given M' -> M -> M'' -> 0, tensoring yields M'⊗N -> M⊗N -> M''⊗N -> 0 exact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important exercise: show right-exactness and note tensor product is not left-exact (example using Z and Z/(2)). Repeated and used later in §1.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product commutation properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Tensor product commutes with certain constructions: it commutes with localization ((S^{-1}A) ⊗_A M ≅ S^{-1}M), with finite products (direct sums) and with arbitrary direct sums; it does not necessarily commute with infinite products or Hom in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: 1.3.L shows localization commutes with ⊗, 1.3.F and 1.3.M treat products and direct sums. Remark: localization commutes with Hom when the first argument is finitely presented (see later exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibered product / pullback (universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given α: X → Z and β: Y → Z, the fibered product X ×_Z Y with projections pr_X, pr_Y is an object universal for maps to X and Y whose compositions to Z agree: maps W→X and W→Y with same composition to Z factor uniquely through W→X×_Z Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique up to unique isomorphism. Interpret concretely in Sets as {(x,y) ∈ X×Y : α(x)=β(y)}. Many exercises (fibered products of sets, open sets, towers of Cartesian diagrams, 'magic diagram').

rubrics_metrics.name: Coproducts and fibered coproducts (pushouts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coproduct is the arrow-reversed notion to product; in Sets coproduct = disjoint union. Fibered coproducts (pushouts) are obtained by reversing the arrows of fibered products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation and exercises: show coproduct for Sets is disjoint union; for rings, B ⊗_A C gives the fibered coproduct/pushout (exercise 1.3.U).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushout of rings via tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: For ring maps A -> B and A -> C, the tensor product B ⊗_A C has a natural ring structure and the canonical maps B -> B⊗_A C and C -> B⊗_A C give the fibered coproduct (pushout) in rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.3.U: check the ring structure and universal property; note the map B -> B⊗_A C is not necessarily injective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monomorphism (categorical injective)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X -> Y is a monomorphism if for any object Z and any two maps μ1, μ2: Z -> X with π∘μ1 = π∘μ2, one has μ1 = μ2. Equivalently, Mor(Z,X) -> Mor(Z,Y) is injective for all Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: categorical analogue of injective maps. Exercise: π is mono iff the diagonal map X -> X ×_Y X is an isomorphism; composition of monos is mono; use magic diagram to relate monos and fibered products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epimorphism (categorical surjective, dual notion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epimorphism is the arrow-reversed notion to monomorphism; intuitively a categorical surjection though in concrete categories epi need not be surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning/example: Z -> Q is an epimorphism in Rings but not surjective as a map of sets. Use caution when translating intuition from sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functors and Yoneda's Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: For object A in C, the contravariant functor h_A : C -> Sets given by h_A(C) = Mor(C, A) determines A up to unique isomorphism. Yoneda's Lemma relates natural transformations between h_A and h_{A'} to morphisms A' -> A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.3.Y: show if natural maps i_C : Mor(C,A) -> Mor(C,A') commute with composition maps then they are induced by a unique g: A -> A'. If bijections, g is iso. Exercise 1.3.Z: bijection between Nat(h_A, h_B) and Mor(B, A) and the analogous contravariant statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits (definition via universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a diagram F: I -> C, a limit lim_{←I} A_i is an object with maps to each A_i compatible with the diagram and universal (final) with this property: any other compatible family W -> A_i factors uniquely through W -> lim A_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility condition spelled in (1.4.1.1). Examples: products, fibered products, p-adic integers Z_p as an inverse limit of Z/p^n. Exercises: existence checks in Set-like categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colimits (dual definition to limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colimit is the arrow-reversed notion: given F: I -> C, colimit lim_{→I} A_i is universal (initial) among objects receiving compatible maps from the A_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Q as colimit of Z -> 1/n Z, unions as colimits of subsets, filtered colimits in Sets and modules constructed via disjoint unions modulo relation. Colimits behave differently from limits; exercises 1.4.C–1.4.G give constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtered colimit construction (Sets and modules)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I is filtered, the colimit in Sets is the disjoint union ⊔_i A_i modulo the equivalence: (a_i,i) ∼ (a_j,j) iff there exists k with maps f: A_i -> A_k, g: A_j -> A_k with f(a_i)=g(a_j). In modules, add module structure and quotient by elements becoming 0 later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.4.D describes the equivalence relation; 1.4.E and 1.4.G verify module structure and well-definedness. Use this to interpret localizations as colimits (1.4.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjoint functors (definition via natural bijection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functors F: A -> B and G: B -> A are adjoint (F left-adjoint to G) if there is a natural bijection τ_{A,B}: Mor_B(F(A), B) ≅ Mor_A(A, G(B)) natural in A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturality conditions spelled in (1.5.0.2). From adjunction derive unit maps η_A: A -> G F(A) and counit ϵ_B: F G(B) -> B with standard compositions giving how τ is computed. Key examples: tensor-Hom adjunction Hom_A(M⊗N, P) ≅ Hom_A(M, Hom_A(N,P)), induction-restriction, suspension-loop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit and counit characterization of adjunction (triangle identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjunction may be characterized by natural transformations η: id_A -> G F and ϵ: F G -> id_B satisfying the triangle identities (e.g., Gϵ ∘ ηG = id_G, Fη ∘ ϵF = id_F), which ensure the bijection between Hom-sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.5.B constructs η_A and ϵ_B from τ. The unit/counit viewpoint gives an alternative (often convenient) way to verify adjunctions.
